doc.title: Derek Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 29, 1995

title: Hired and fired by Benny Goodman, 1962 South America tour
summary: Smith praises Goodman's clarinet, describes his difficult nature and how he was fired and rehired before a tour.

story.theme_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the leader and his bands
story.community_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader

blocks.x: Well, what do you want to know? It’s hard to say. I mean without a doubt, Benny was the finest jazz clarinetist — this is all subjective opinion, certainly my opinion — I’ve never heard of anybody that played as well as he did that thrilled me as well. But, given all that, which is a big given, he was a very difficult guy to get along with. None of us really knew why. Either he heard — they say that symphony conductors hear what they want to hear of a piece a fraction of a second before the orchestra plays it, and then if the orchestra doesn’t play it exactly the way they hear it in their heads, then they get upset. And I think it was something like that with Benny. He heard exactly what he thought it was going to be. And then if the band, if it wasn’t exactly the same, he’d get upset and he would start pointing at people. But anyway, it all doesn’t matter. Benny’s been dead some years now, and all the music, there’s so many records of it and it will live forever. It’s wonderful music. But the first time I went with him, it was in 1962. I hadn’t been in the country that long. And I needed the job, simply to be associated with somebody of that stature. So my friend, he’s dead now, the drummer Mousey Alexander, a good friend of mine, he said, “I’ll get you on with Benny.” So I made all the rehearsals and read the “Stealing Apples” — you know the thing, the lovely — just kept my nose clean and didn’t say anything. But then, the night, we were going to go to South America the next day, that was the tour. And so 7:30 the night before we were supposed to go, the manager called me up. He said, “listen, listen carefully.” He said, “Benny’s going to call in five minutes and he’s going to fire you.” I said, “what! What have I done! I haven’t said anything, I haven’t done anything bad.” He said, no, but he’s going to fire you. But here’s what you say. You say well it’s all right, Benny, you can fire me, but for the period of three weeks that we’re going to be away I’ve turned down a lot of work, so I feel that you’ve got to pay me the money that you promised me. And he said, “then he’ll hire you again.” Five minutes later the phone rings. He says “well, look Pops, it’s not working out. You’d better forget it.” So I said, “well okay, Mista..mista..mista Go..go..go..go..Goodman,” I said, “okay, I understand, but I’ve turned down all this wo..wo..wo..wo..work, and I feel you sh..sh..should pay me for it.” And he says, “okay, you’d better come with us.” And I mean that’s exactly how it happened.
